passage:
"Kavitha, she's not eating," Papa murmured.
"Shalini, what's the matter?" said Amma.
"Rohan didn't even say well done," Shalini said, pushing rice around her plate. "He walked away when the teacher gave me the certificate."
"Maybe he's hurting. He wanted that quiz cup too, no?"
"But I didn't do anything wrong! Now I feel bad for winning. Should I have lost?"
"Did you cheat?"
"No!"
"Then you owe no apology for winning. But you can be kind."
Shalini thought. "I could leave him alone at lunch tomorrow. Not chase him."
"And?"
"And tell him I like sitting with him, whenever he wants. Amma, will he still be my friend?"
"Give it time."
Shalini nodded and finally took a bite.

qa.q: What did Rohan do when the teacher gave Shalini the certificate?
What is Shalini feeling about her win, and why?
qa.a: She feels confused and a bit guilty, because Rohan went cold and she wonders if she should have lost.

qa.q: What plan did Shalini make for tomorrow, and why is it a kind one?
qa.a: She will leave him alone at lunch and tell him she likes sitting with him whenever he wants. Giving space without pushing keeps the friendship open. 🙂

qa.q: What might Rohan be going through?
qa.a: He wanted the quiz cup too, so he is probably hurting and disappointed, not necessarily angry at Shalini.

grounding: Shows a child confused and guilty after a friend goes cold over her win, deciding to give space and stay kind.

passage:
Tuesday: Irawati's essay won the district prize. Her best friend Irfan, who had entered too, walked out of the hall without a word.
Wednesday: At lunch Irfan sat with other boys. When Irawati said hi, he just nodded. She felt confused, then guilty. Should she not have entered? Was winning a crime?
She almost stopped mentioning the prize at all. Instead she decided to give him space for a day, and stay kind.
Friday: She slipped a note into his bag: "Your essay about your grandfather made me cry. You matter more to me than any certificate. Carrom at five?"
At five, Irfan knocked. "Sorry," he mumbled, not looking up. "I was jealous. Congrats." She set up the board. He won the first game, and she didn't mind at all.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel when Irfan just nodded at lunch?
qa.a: Confused and guilty, wondering whether winning was a crime.

qa.q: How did Irawati handle Irfan's coldness?
qa.a: She gave him space, stayed kind, and sent a note praising his essay and inviting him to carrom.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling behind his coldness?
qa.a: He was jealous of her win, as he admitted when he apologised.

grounding: A girl whose friend goes cold after she wins a contest feels confused and guilty, gives him space and reminds him their friendship matters.

passage: Jeevan, your friend Aman won't talk to you since you won the quiz? Sit with your Jagdish Dadaji. When I was eleven, I won the Makar Sankranti kite contest in our mohalla. My best friend Mohan came second. That evening he didn't come to the terrace. The next day he walked past me as if I were a lamp-post. I felt terrible and confused, almost wished I had lost. My Bapuji said, "Don't take back your win, and don't chase him. Give him a few days, and be kind." So I waited. On the fourth day I took the prize, a huge red fighter kite, to his house. "It flies better with two," I said. He looked at it a long time. Then he fetched his manja. We flew it together till dark. So, Jeevan, stay kind and give Aman some time.

qa.q: What was the prize for the kite contest?
How did young Jagdish feel when Mohan walked past him?
qa.a: Terrible and confused, almost wishing he had lost.

qa.q: What choice in Dadaji's story mended the friendship?
qa.a: Waiting a few days and then offering to fly the prize kite together.

qa.q: Why might Mohan have walked past as if Jagdish were a lamp-post?
qa.a: He was probably jealous and hurt about coming second.

grounding: A grandfather recalls a friend going cold after he won a contest, and how giving space and staying kind mended the friendship.
